common_name: Canyon Creek Abelia (Copper New-Growth Arching Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Canyon Creek's arching, cascading branches show off best when given room to spread rather than being sheared into a formal hedge.

directions: Canyon Creek is an abelia selection prized for foliage that emerges a rich copper-orange in spring, matures to yellow-green with darker green centers through summer, and warms again to bronze-copper tones in cool fall weather, giving three-season color on the same graceful, arching, cascading branch structure typical of larger abelia cultivars. Small, fragrant, white, tubular flowers appear in loose clusters from late spring through frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds, and the plant's spreading habit makes it a good choice for a mixed border or slope where its weeping branch tips can drape naturally. Like other abelias it tolerates clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established, needing only an occasional thinning of old wood after the main spring flush to keep it looking fresh.

common_name: Twist of Lime Abelia (Lime-and-Cream Variegated Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; variegation is brightest with several hours of direct sun, and new growth flushes pink before settling into its lime-and-cream pattern.

directions: Twist of Lime is an abelia selection grown chiefly for its foliage, small leaves margined in creamy yellow around a lime-green center, with new growth emerging flushed pink before settling into the mature variegated pattern, giving the shrub a bright, multicolored look through most of the growing season. It still produces the small, fragrant, white-to-pale-pink tubular flowers typical of abelia from late spring into fall on gracefully arching stems, and like other abelia cultivars it is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought with minimal care once established. Prune lightly after the main flush of spring bloom if shaping is wanted, and watch for occasional reversion shoots of plain green foliage, which should be cut out to keep the variegation strong.

common_name: Ever Red Loropetalum (Dwarf Mounding Red-Leaf Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ever Red's naturally dwarf, mounding habit needs little to no pruning to hold a tidy shape in a small bed or foundation planting.

directions: Ever Red is a dwarf, densely mounding loropetalum selection that holds a compact size well below the larger, more vigorous fringe flower cultivars, making it a practical choice for small foundation beds where standard loropetalum quickly becomes too large. Its small leaves emerge burgundy-red and hold that deep color better through summer heat than many red-leaf loropetalum selections, set off by frilly, spidery magenta-pink flowers concentrated in spring with lighter scattered rebloom later in the season. Like other loropetalum it is easygoing in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, needing only an occasional light shaping right after the main spring bloom to stay tidy.

common_name: Carolina Midnight Loropetalum (Near-Black Purple Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina Midnight holds its darkest foliage color in full sun and grows vigorously enough to need an annual shaping to control size in smaller beds.

directions: Carolina Midnight is a vigorous, large-growing loropetalum selected for exceptionally dark, near-black purple foliage that holds its intensity through the growing season better than many purple-leaf loropetalum cultivars, which tend to fade toward green in summer heat. Frilly, spidery, deep magenta-pink flowers stand out sharply against the near-black leaves in a heavy spring flush, with lighter rebloom into fall. Its large mature size makes it best suited to a screen, background planting, or small tree form rather than a tight foundation bed; like other loropetalum it tolerates heat, humidity, and normal garden soil well as long as drainage is adequate, and should be pruned, if needed, right after the spring bloom to avoid cutting off the next flush of flower buds.

common_name: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink Loropetalum (Compact Purple-Leaf Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the compact Jazz Hands series holds a tidy rounded shape naturally and needs little pruning beyond an occasional light shaping right after the spring bloom.

directions: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink is a compact member of the Jazz Hands loropetalum series, bred to fit small beds and container plantings while still delivering the deep burgundy-purple foliage and ribbon-like, spidery pink flowers the species is known for. Its dense, well-branched, rounded habit stays smaller than most loropetalum cultivars, holding good foliage color through the season with a heavy spring flower flush and scattered rebloom later on. It shares the easy care of other loropetalum selections, tolerating normal garden soil, heat, and humidity as long as drainage is good, and needs only minimal shaping right after its main bloom period to stay neat.
